sites.name: Argo Mill
overview: Above Clear Creek in Idaho Springs stands the seven-story Argo Mill, built to process ore carried out of the nearby Argo Tunnel. Starting in 1913, it used gravity and innovative ore-concentration equipment to turn lower-grade ore from surrounding mines into material worth shipping to smelters. Its work ended after a devastating underground flood in 1943. Today the distinctive mill survives as a historic industrial landmark and visitor attraction. Scan the mill building itself; the nearby Argo Tunnel portal is a separate feature.

timeline.text: Work began on Samuel Newhouse's mine-drainage and ore-transportation tunnel, later known as the Argo Tunnel.
The Argo Tunnel was completed, bringing ore from connected mines toward Idaho Springs.
Construction began on the large seven-story Argo ore-concentration mill beside the tunnel outlet.
Argo Reduction and Ore Purchasing Company began milling operations.
A contemporary engineering journal praised the mill's innovative metallurgical process; the National Register nomination describes approximately 300 tons/day capacity.
A deadly flooding accident associated with the Argo underground workings ended tunnel and mill operations.
Argo Tunnel and Mill was listed in the National Register of Historic Places (78000836).

moreHistory: Construction of the Argo Mill began in June 1912; the Argo Reduction and Ore Purchasing Company began processing ore in April 1913. The mill stood at the outlet of Samuel Newhouse's Argo drainage and haulage tunnel, completed in 1910, which helped sustain deep mining in the Central City–Idaho Springs area. According to the original National Register nomination, the mill's large seven-story, steel-framed corrugated-iron building was designed around gravity-fed ore concentration and could handle roughly 300 tons per day. Ore originally came from the Gunnell, Prize, Ophir and Poco mines; later the Gem, Sun and Moon and smaller mines also supplied ore. Its advanced process combined wet stamping, chemical treatment, amalgamation and concentrating tables, allowing lower-grade sulphide ore to be shipped economically to smelters. On January 19, 1943, a deadly underground flooding accident shut down the tunnel and mill. The surviving mill and equipment became a preservation and visitor-education site; the combined Argo Tunnel and Mill was listed in the National Register on January 31, 1978. These are facts about the MILL's role, not claims that the mill was itself a producing underground mine.

sites.name: Argo Tunnel
overview: At this Idaho Springs portal, miners began a four-mile tunnel in 1893 to drain deep gold mines and bring ore out by rail. Originally called the Newhouse Tunnel, it eventually reached toward Central City and helped keep mines operating far below the surface. A fatal flood in 1943 ended the mining era, but water continued flowing from the tunnel. Today the entrance is part of the historic Argo complex, while a nearby treatment plant handles the metal-rich drainage. The Argo Mill is a separate historic structure.

timeline.text: Samuel Newhouse's drainage-and-haulage tunnel project began from Idaho Springs, first by hand then with powered drills.
Tunnel reached its final 21,968-foot terminus under Eureka Gulch after intermittent construction.
The associated Argo ore mill was constructed at the tunnel complex and began milling in April 1913; it is a separate physical site.
A flood triggered by work on a lateral to the Kansas shaft killed four miners and ended operations.
Argo Tunnel and Mill listed in National Register of Historic Places (NRIS 78000836).
Argo water-treatment plant began full operation treating metal-rich tunnel discharge.

moreHistory: The Argo (originally Newhouse) Tunnel was conceived by mining promoter Samuel Newhouse to solve the costly water, ventilation and ore-transport problems of deep gold mines between Idaho Springs and Central City. Work started at the Idaho Springs portal in September 1893. Intermittent driving ended November 18, 1910 at 21,968 feet (4.16 miles) under Eureka Gulch. The tunnel followed a gentle drainage grade, carried a rail haulage system, and opened deep connections to mines across Clear Creek and Gilpin Counties; the 1978 National Register nomination describes the first 13,100 feet as 8 by 8 feet, with smaller dimensions farther in. An associated ore mill began operating in April 1913, but the tunnel portal is a separate historic feature. On January 19, 1943, water broke into the tunnel from work on a lateral near the Kansas shaft, killing four miners and ending operations. The tunnel continued discharging metal-rich water after closure. EPA's Argo treatment plant began operation April 7, 1998, treating discharge collected just outside the portal. The historic tunnel and mill complex is on the National Register of Historic Places; the portal is now interpreted as part of the Argo visitor experience.

sites.name: Capital Prize Mine
overview: At the edge of Georgetown, the Capital Prize Mine tells the story of miners tunneling deep beneath Griffith Mountain in search of gold and silver. A 1915 engineer's report describes a remarkable crosscut, two tunnel mouths, a mill, and an ambitious ventilation project that struggled against poor air and difficult rock. Today the surviving mine complex is operated as a guided underground tour. The app's location marks the signed public visitor area, not an invitation to enter historic workings independently.

timeline.text: George and David Griffith discovered mineralization near Georgetown; later Capital Prize operators trace the mine's origins to their Griffith district claims.
A Griffith location certificate for the Mills County Lode was filed January 4; a later Capital Prize engineering account connects the claim history to the mine group.
The long Capital Prize crosscut adit was started from the Georgetown town edge to reach the Aetna vein at depth.
A concentrator mill was built to treat ore from the Capital operation.
Ritter documented the two-mouth crosscut, the Aetna-vein workings, and an unsuccessful 877-foot ventilation raise.
Major industrial operations had largely ceased, though later small leasing and intermittent work continued.
A town special-use permit supported renewed rehabilitation; the operator's engineering compilation records 1,440 feet of main tunnel rehabilitated.
The operator reports reopening for public tours after rehabilitation.

moreHistory: The Griffith brothers' mining claims helped launch Georgetown's mining district in the 1860s. The later Capital Mining and Tunnel Company drove a long crosscut from the town edge beginning around 1905 to reach the Aetna vein at depth. In January 1915 mining engineer Etienne A. Ritter described two branches near the tunnel mouth: a south entrance serving the rock dump and compressor house and a north entrance serving the mill and outbuildings. The long branch reached the Aetna vein after about 3,520 feet; the company extended the crosscut beyond that intersection and drifted along the vein. Ventilation was a major obstacle: an 877-foot raise could not be completed because of poor air, and a borehole drilled from above lost its tools. A concentrator mill built in 1907 treated ore, but heavy development expenses and unstable ground burdened the operation. Later engineering records say major operations ceased around 1918 while smaller lease work continued intermittently, and document rehabilitation of 1,440 feet of the main access tunnel after a 1983 Georgetown permit. The mine was later reopened as a guided visitor attraction. The Aetna/Comet lode and nearby mine claims are related geological context, not alternate names for the Capital Prize portal.

sites.name: Centennial Mill
overview: Georgetown last surviving ore mill was rebuilt in 1929, used flotation processing and has been preserved since 2004.

timeline.text: Relocated and rebuilt
Acquired for preservation

moreHistory: Western States Mining Company relocated and rebuilt the former Griffith Mill in 1929 by the Colorado Central Railroad. The mill used flotation ore processing. Historic Georgetown acquired it in 2004; Colorado State Historical Fund awarded acquisition/stabilization support under site 5CC.3.333. No tours.

sites.name: Crazy Girl Mine
overview: The Crazy Girl Mine worked a gold-, silver-, lead-, zinc- and copper-bearing vein on Alps Mountain. Miners sank a shaft serving three underground levels and added a separate crosscut tunnel. From 1902 to 1952, intermittent operations shipped 1,928 tons of ore. In 1952, falling lead prices abruptly ended a period of production. The USGS mapped the mine's shaft and described the mineral-rich vein. Remnant marks the historically mapped shaft location; whether any opening or structure survives there has not been verified. Mine workings are hazardous, and no public access is implied.

timeline.text: Intermittent documented ore production; total 1,928 tons shipped during this period.
USGS geologists documented the shaft, three underground levels, separate Crazy Girl crosscut, and incomplete Baby Eddy tunnel connection.
Mine shut down abruptly after a drop in the price of lead.
Harrison and Wells published their geological and historical account of the Freeland-Lamartine district.

moreHistory: USGS Harrison and Wells (1954) documented the Crazy Girl Mine as a shaft connected to workings on three levels, with a separate crosscut tunnel into the first level. The Baby Eddy tunnel was driven toward the third level but was never completed; it is a distinct portal. The shaft collar was about 9,700 ft elevation. Production records show intermittent operation between 1902 and 1952 and 1,928 tons of ore shipped, yielding 231 oz gold, 6,885 oz silver, 4,591 lb copper, 412,818 lb lead, and 73,881 lb zinc. At the 1952 USGS visit, K. J. King and J. M. East of Boulder leased the mine and ore was being removed from a second-level stope. Falling lead prices caused an abrupt shutdown in July 1952. USGS described a northeast-striking Crazy Girl vein with pyrite, chalcopyrite, tetrahedrite, galena and sphalerite; ore occurred in irregular lenses and pods. Nearby Yankee Girl and Belle Creole workings lie along possible vein extensions but are not the Crazy Girl shaft or its scan target. Current remains, access, and safety are not established.

sites.name: Dunkirk Mine
overview: The Dunkirk Mine was a significant nineteenth-century silver working above Silver Plume. By about 1880 it reportedly employed 70 people and had a shaft nearly 600 feet deep. Its main entrance is documented in federal mine records, although the entrance may no longer be visible.

timeline.text: Contemporary history reports about 70 workers, nearly 600-foot main shaft, at least 1,800 feet of underground levels and approximately $130,000 in recent production.
U.S. Mint annual report names Dunkirk as a producing Republican Mountain mine.
U.S. Bureau of Mines MRDS record documents Dunkirk main-entrance position.
Dan A. Polhemus documents Dunkirk eastern tailings.

moreHistory: Contemporary historian Aaron Frost described the Dunkirk Mine east of Dives and west of Pay Rock on Republican Mountain. He reported ownership by Herman Silver Mining Company of New York and supervision by Charles H. Morris. After seven years of development before profitable ore, the mine reportedly yielded about $130,000 in just over a year. By about 1880, it employed 70 workers and had a main shaft nearly 600 feet deep with at least 1,800 feet of levels. An 1880 US Mint report separately lists Dunkirk among Republican Mountain silver workings. A 1983 U.S. Bureau of Mines record identifies Dunkirk as a past-producing underground silver mine. Site-specific eastern tailings were photographed in 2019.

sites.name: Lebanon Mill
overview: Lebanon Mill crushed and sampled ore using water power. Patented in 1872, it was rebuilt for Georgetown Loop interpretation in 1978.

timeline.text: Mill patented.
Mill leased.
National Register listing.
Mill rebuilt.

moreHistory: The 1971 NPS nomination describes a two-story 30-by-60-foot wooden mill. Ore was received below, lifted, jaw-crushed, sampled and bagged upstairs. Clear Creek water drove a wheel; the adjacent dam crossed the creek. Superintendent Julius G. Pohle patented the mill in 1872, processing Lebanon Mine and custom ore, then leased it in 1877. Its closure date is unknown. Excavations found outbuilding foundations in 1970. Listed in 1971, the mill was rebuilt in 1978.

sites.name: Lebanon Mine Tunnel
overview: The Lebanon Tunnel was driven into Republican Mountain in 1870 as part of Georgetown's silver boom. Its workings reached about 1,200 feet by 1886, and it is still recognizable by its signed portal. Preservation efforts reopened the tunnel in 1969 and restored the surrounding mine buildings in 1978. The mine is now visited only through the Georgetown Loop Railroad's guided tours.

timeline.text: Lebanon Mining Company drives tunnel into Republican Mountain.
Lebanon among approximately 50 Georgetown mines producing ore.
Tunnel approximately 1,200 feet; Hise Lode reached at 1,100 feet.
Preservation crews clear and light Lebanon tunnel; discover associated building footprints.
Reconstructed Lebanon mine buildings open to public.

moreHistory: History Colorado records the Lebanon Mining Company driving the Lebanon Tunnel into Republican Mountain in 1870. Clear Creek County tourism says Lebanon was among about 50 Georgetown-area mines producing ore in 1885. In 1886 its tunnel extended approximately 1,200 feet and met the Hise Lode around 1,100 feet from the portal; work ended late that decade amid falling silver prices. Preservation crews cleared and lit the Lebanon tunnel in 1969, locating former blacksmith shop, miners' dry, manager office and tool shed footprints. Reconstructed mine buildings opened in 1978. Today the railroad operator leads visitors 500 feet, or over 1,000 feet on extended tours, into the historic tunnel. The Lebanon Mill and Everett Tunnel are separate resources.

sites.name: Little Emma Tunnel
overview: Little Emma was a small gold, silver, lead and zinc mine in Virginia Canyon above Idaho Springs. Although its adit was short, federal records document ore shipments in 1912 and 1921–1926. USGS geologists mapped the narrow mineralized veins underground. A later state survey identified the mine’s separate waste-rock pile and building remnants, distinct from the neighboring Brighton Mine. The historic site is mapped, but the current condition of the tunnel entrance is unknown.

timeline.text: USGS records a small ore shipment from the Little Emma adit.
U.S. Bureau of Mines records 56 tons of crude ore shipped, yielding gold, silver, lead and zinc.
Idaho Springs Sampling Works records additional ore assays from the Little Emma workings.
USGS publishes a mine-specific description and underground plan (fig. 54).
Colorado reclamation survey identifies Little Emma as site #108, documenting its waste-rock pile and building remnants.

moreHistory: USGS identifies Little Emma as a short drift adit in Virginia Canyon at about 8,690 feet. A small shipment occurred in 1912. Bureau of Mines figures record 56 tons of crude ore shipped from 1921 through 1926, yielding 27 troy ounces of gold, 1,616 troy ounces of silver, 22,398 pounds of lead and 2,223 pounds of zinc. The adit cuts granite gneiss, pegmatite and biotite gneiss; narrow, branching veins contain pyrite, chalcopyrite, galena, sphalerite and quartz. The 1966 USGS report includes a plan of the workings (fig. 54) and ore assay records including 1930. A 2001 Colorado reclamation report separately identified Little Emma site #108 beside Brighton #41, documenting about 1,000 cubic yards of Little Emma waste rock and the remains of a building then visible from the old road. The report describes erosion affecting waste rock in Boomerang Gulch. No claim is made that the historic portal or structures survive today.

sites.name: Phoenix Gold Mine
overview: Opened in 1871, Phoenix Gold Mine preserves underground gold-mining workings near Idaho Springs. The Mosch family discovered the Resurrection Vein in the 1970s and has offered guided tours since 1988. Visitor access is controlled by the operator.

timeline.text: Mine opened
Mosch family acquisition, per operator
Resurrection Vein discovery
Public tours began

moreHistory: Opened in 1871, Phoenix was worked in several periods by successive operators. Phoenix No. 1 and No. 2 and a mill site were reportedly patented in 1875. The Mosch family reports buying the mine in 1968. In the 1970s David and Cyndi Mosch identified the Resurrection Vein, a new gold-bearing occurrence within the Phoenix workings. Underground crosscut work followed in the 1980s, and public tours began in 1988. Clear Creek tourism identifies both Phoenix and Resurrection veins at the site. Some secondary accounts disagree about exact ownership dates.

sites.name: Silver King Mine
overview: The Silver King Mine near Dumont had upper and lower tunnels following an ore-bearing vein. USGS mapped its workings in 1952 and recorded shipments of gold, silver, copper, lead and zinc from 1944 to 1947. The historic lower portal site is the scan target; its present-day condition is unknown.

timeline.text: 1353 tons of ore shipped from Silver King group.
USGS mapped upper and lower portals and underground vein.

moreHistory: USGS recorded 1353 tons shipped 1944-47 containing 25 oz gold, 1900 oz silver, 3630 lb copper, 52692 lb lead and 5280 lb zinc. The main vein was mapped for about 1200 ft, with galena-sphalerite ore concentrated near 500 ft inward. The lower and upper portals were mapped in 1952; the Silver King Extension is separate.

sites.name: Urad Mine
overview: The Urad Mine was an important Colorado molybdenum producer. Its story stretches from World War I-era mining through major expansion in the 1960s and closure in 1974. Today the mine is sealed and the area has undergone extensive reclamation. Nearby Henderson is a separate, deeper deposit.

timeline.text: Substantial development began.
Primos Chemical shipped concentrates.
Mine and 200-ton-per-day mill operated.
AMAX restarted large-scale production.
Urad mine closed and was sealed.

moreHistory: Urad was developed beginning in 1914. Primos Chemical shipped molybdenum concentrates in 1918-1919. Vanadium Corporation bought the property in 1921. The mine reopened in 1941, with a 200-ton-per-day mill in 1944-1946. AMAX leased it in 1961, purchased it in 1963, and restarted large-scale mining in 1967. Nearly 48 to 50 million pounds of molybdenum were produced before depletion and closure in 1974. Six underground levels were developed, including the A portal level at about 10280 feet. The portal was sealed and the tailings reclaimed. The related Henderson orebody lies deeper and is a separate operation.
